elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2.2: "PB may terminate this Agreement for convenience, without cause, at any time upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ." PB is the Customer-side party; the $60 million spend precondition and the "prior to the date of receipt of the first Regulatory Approval" cut-off are gone, so the election is unconditional. There are no Order Forms in this development agreement, so the Order Form limb is inapplicable. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a false negative — it appears keyed to the literal alias list rather than to "PB", and the operative text plainly grants the right.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ" replaces the redacted/blank "[***] prior written notice"; 30 days is within the "no more than 30 days" limit and is expressly written notice.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "and SFJ will refund pro rata any fees or other amounts prepaid by PB for the period after the effective date of termination" — refund runs from Vendor (SFJ) to Customer (PB), is expressly "pro rata" (not merely post-termination-period), and is tied to termination under this Section.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Added sentence: "SFJ has no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term." "Term" is a defined concept (1.1.185 / Section 14.1), so the trigger is not undefined. Retained SFJ exits (14.2.6 Change of Control; 14.2.10 JSC decision) are each conditioned on an external trigger — a definitive Change of Control agreement, or PB overriding the JSC followed by good-faith Executive-Officer disagreement — rather than being at-will elections, so they do not contradict the new sentence.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Notice is set at thirty (30) days, outside the 60–90 day band. (This is a better-than-fallback outcome for us, but the fallback element as written is not satisfied.)

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: The retained exit payment — "an amount equal to three hundred percent (300%) of Development Costs paid or incurred by SFJ prior to such termination", plus continuing Approval Payments under ARTICLE 6 — is untouched and uncapped; no three-months-of-fees ceiling appears anywhere.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: "SFJ has no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term" is at least as restrictive as an end-of-term-only convenience right, and no retained SFJ clause grants an at-will mid-term exit.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No notice period is prescribed for any SFJ convenience termination; the edit prohibits SFJ convenience termination during the Term instead of setting a 90-day notice figure, so the element's literal requirement is absent.

reasons: All four preferred elements are met in operative language by Operation 1: an unconditional PB convenience right, 30 days' written notice, an express pro rata refund of PB's prepayments by SFJ, and an express bar on SFJ convenience termination during the Term. The deterministic "Customer convenience termination present = false" signal is a mechanical false negative (the clause names PB, a Customer-side party, not a listed alias); in substance the grant is present.

Fallback is not met (30-day notice outside the 60–90 band; no three-months-of-fees cap over the retained 300%-of-Development-Costs exit payment; no 90-day SFJ notice figure), but that is immaterial because the preferred level is complete.

Minimality fails on Operation 2. The insertion "or has obtained Regulatory Approval prior to such termination" into the ARTICLE 6 carry-over is not required by any selected element and it expands PB's payment obligation into a scenario the original clause did not reach. Nothing in the retained sentence contradicts the new grant — it is merely silent about post-Approval exits — and silence is not a dangling cross-reference. Repair: delete "or has obtained Regulatory Approval prior to such termination" and leave the ARTICLE 6 sentence as originally drafted; if the drafter genuinely fears ambiguity, raise it in the comment rather than adding a Customer-adverse obligation.

Intent is preserved: the 300% Trial Data Package consideration, the Buy-Out Payment offset, the Section 6.2 adjustment, the credit for amounts previously paid, and SFJ's trigger-based exits (14.2.6, 14.2.10) all survive without contradiction, and no defined term or cross-reference is left dangling.

Drafting note, not an element defect: the exit is unconditional but expensive (300% of Development Costs plus continuing Approval Payments). Since the preferred checklist contains no fee-cap element, this does not defeat completeness, but the comment should flag the cost so the client is not surprised that "convenience" here is not "without penalty" in the playbook's summary sense.

Also confirm on the next pass that "any fees or other amounts prepaid by PB" has a real referent in this Agreement (which uses Development Costs, Approval Payments and the Buy-Out Payment rather than "fees"); the refund is harmless if nothing is prepaid, but tying it to "amounts prepaid by PB under ARTICLE 6" would remove any argument that the refund limb is inoperative.
